The definition of a learning machine is: A computer program learns with accumulating experience regarding a class of tasks T and a performance measure P, if its performance on these tasks (according to P) improves as it gains new experience.
This definition is very general.
The course will consider various algorithms that solve specific tasks and perform better with more initial (test) data.
Today's lecture will discuss the general theory of Bayesian inference, which is usually applicable to any machine learning algorithm.
The lecture will first provide a brief overview of basic ML tasks.
Supervised learning is learning with a set of labeled examples.
In supervised learning, there is a training set, which is a set of examples, each consisting of features (attributes).
In supervised learning, examples have correct answers, which is a variable (response) we want to predict; it can be categorical, continuous, or ordinal.
In supervised learning, a model learns from this dataset during the training phase (learning phase), then it can be applied to new examples (test set).
The main goal of supervised learning is to train a model that not only fits training data but also generalizes well to new data.
If a model does not generalize well to new data, this is called overfitting.
In supervised learning, usually we’re given only the training set.
Cross-validation is a method to check model generalization by splitting data into training and validation sets.
Typically, preprocessing is performed before inputting data, extracting the most informative aspects (feature extraction).
Classification is a supervised learning task where there is a discrete set of categories (classes), and new examples must be assigned to a class.
Examples of classification include text classification by topics, spam filtering, and face/object/text recognition.
Regression is a supervised learning task where there is an unknown function whose values we must predict for new examples.
Examples of regression include engineering applications (predicting temperature, robot position, etc.), finance (predicting stock prices), and speech recognition (with temporal changes).
Unsupervised learning is learning without labeled data, only raw data.
Clustering is a type of unsupervised learning that partitions data into unknown classes based on similarity.

Examples of clustering include identifying gene families from nucleotide sequences, user clustering and personalization, and clustering mass spectrometry images into segments with different compositions.

Dimensionality reduction is a type of unsupervised learning where data has huge dimensionality (many features), and we need to reduce it by selecting the most informative features so algorithms can run effectively.
Matrix completion is a type of unsupervised learning where, given a sparse matrix, we predict missing values.
Semi-supervised learning is often used when some data has labeled examples.
Reinforcement learning is a type of learning where an agent learns from its own trials and errors.
Multi-armed bandits is a problem in reinforcement learning where one chooses from several actions, each leading to random outcomes, with the goal to maximize rewards.
In reinforcement learning, there is a trade-off called exploration versus exploitation: deciding when to explore new options versus exploiting known ones.
Credit assignment is a problem in reinforcement learning where a reward is given at the end (e.g., winning a game), and we must assign credit to each action leading to success.
Active learning involves choosing the next (relatively expensive) test.
Learning to rank is ordinal regression to produce ordered lists (e.g., internet search).
Bootstrapping is reusing the results of a model to improve itself.
Model selection is finding the balance between models with many or few parameters.

All methods and approaches benefit from methods that not only give answers but also estimate model confidence, data description quality, and anticipate how these measures change with further experiments.
Probability theory plays a central role in machine learning, and we will actively use it.
The course will not require detailed mathematical definitions of sigma-algebras, probability measures, Borel sets, etc.
For the course, it suffices to understand discrete random variables, where probabilities sum to one, and continuous random variables, where the integral of the nonnegative density equals one.
Joint probability is the probability of two events occurring simultaneously, denoted p(x, y).
Marginalization is the process of summing joint probabilities over one variable: p(x) = sum_y p(x, y).
Conditional probability p(x|y) is the probability of one event given another occurred, and it satisfies p(x, y) = p(x|y)p(y) = p(y|x)p(x).
Bayes’ theorem: p(y|x) = p(x|y)p(y) / p(x) = p(x|y)p(y) / sum_{y'} p(x|y')p(y').
Independence: x and y are independent if p(x, y) = p(x)p(y).
In Bayes’ theorem, p(θ|D) = p(θ)p(D|θ) / p(D), where p(θ) is the prior probability, p(D|θ) is the likelihood, p(θ|D) is the posterior probability, and p(D) = ∫ p(D|θ)p(θ) dθ is the evidence.
In statistics, typically we look for the maximum likelihood hypothesis: θ_ML = arg max_θ p(D|θ).
Bayesian approaches seek the posterior distribution p(θ|D) ∝ p(D|θ)p(θ) and possibly the maximum a posteriori hypothesis: θ_MAP = arg max_θ p(θ|D) = arg max_θ p(D|θ)p(θ).
An example of a direct problem is: an urn contains 10 balls, 3 of which are black; what is the probability of drawing a black ball?
Another direct problem: an urn contains 10 balls numbered from 1 to 10; what’s the probability that the sum of numbers on three consecutively drawn balls is 12?

An example of an inverse problem is: two urns each contain 10 balls; one has 3 black balls, the other 6; someone took a ball from one urn, and it was black; what is the probability it was taken from the first urn?
In the inverse problem, probabilities immediately become Bayesian (although it can also be reformulated through frequencies).
Direct probability problems describe a probabilistic process or model and ask to calculate a specific probability (i.e., predict behavior based on the model).
Inverse problems contain hidden variables (in the example—the number of the urn from which the ball was drawn).
Inverse problems often require building a probabilistic model based on observed behavior.
Machine learning problems typically belong to the category of inverse problems.

Classical probability theory, originating from physical experiments, usually views probability as the limit of the ratio of occurrences of a particular experiment outcome to the total number of experiments.
A standard example of probability as frequency is tossing a coin.
One might want to reason about the probability of events such as Spain winning the FIFA World Cup in 2026, the Odyssey having been written by a woman, and AGI taking over control from humans by 2030.
For such singular events, the notion of experiments repeated to infinity is meaningless because there is exactly one experiment.
In the Bayesian interpretation, probabilities become degrees of belief, as Thomas Bayes originally saw it.
Both the frequentist and Bayesian interpretations of probability follow the same laws.

A simple inference problem involves an unfair coin flipped N times, producing a sequence of results.
In this problem, we must determine the coin's "unfairness" and predict the next outcome.
If the probability of heads is p_h = θ (and thus tails probability p_t = 1−θ), the probability of a sequence s with n heads and m tails is p(s| p_h = θ) = θ^n (1−θ)^m.
The problem assumes a uniform prior for the coin probability before the experiments, meaning no initial preference about θ.
Bayes' theorem is used to infer the hidden parameters.
The likelihood is given by p(θ|s) = p(s|θ) p(θ) / p(s).
Here, p(θ) should be understood as a continuous random variable defined on the interval [0, 1].
The assumption of a uniform distribution means the prior probability p(θ) = 1 for θ∈[0,1].
We already know p(s|θ).
Thus, p(θ|s) = θ^n (1−θ)^m / p(s).
p(s) can be calculated as p(s) = ∫_0^1 θ^n (1−θ)^m dθ.
The integral evaluates to Γ(n+1)Γ(m+1)/Γ(n+m+2).
This simplifies to n! m!/(n+m+1)!.
arg max_θ p(θ|s) = n/(n+m) can be found without this integral.
To predict the next outcome, we calculate p(heads|s) = ∫_0^1 p(heads|θ) p(θ|s) dθ.
This equals ∫_0^1 θ^(n+1) (1−θ)^m / p(s) dθ.
This simplifies to (n+1)! m!/(n+m+2)! · (n+m+1)!/(n! m!).
The result is (n+1)/(n+m+2).
This result is known as Laplace’s rule.

This was an illustration of two main tasks in Bayesian inference: (1) finding the posterior distribution over hypotheses/parameters: p(θ|D) ∝ p(D|θ) p(θ) and/or finding the maximum a posteriori hypothesis θ_MAP = arg max_θ p(θ|D); (2) finding the predictive distribution for outcomes of future experiments: p(x|D) ∝ ∫_{θ∈Θ} p(x|θ) p(D|θ) p(θ) dθ.
The main task in Bayesian inference is to learn the parameters of a distribution and/or to predict its next points from the available data.
Bayesian inference involves the likelihood of the data p(x|θ).
Bayesian inference involves the prior distribution p(θ).
Bayesian inference involves the marginal likelihood p(x) = ∫_Θ p(x|θ) p(θ) dθ.
Bayesian inference involves the posterior distribution p(θ|x) = p(x|θ) p(θ) / p(x).
Bayesian inference involves the prediction for a new x' given by p(x'|x) = ∫_Θ p(x'|θ) p(θ|x) dθ.
The task is usually to find p(θ|x) and/or p(x'|x).
When doing Bayesian inference, besides the likelihood we must also have a prior distribution over all possible values of the parameters.
Prior distributions are very important.
The task of Bayesian inference is to compute p(θ|x) and/or p(x'|x).
To do that, we first have to choose p(θ).
We need to decide how to choose prior distributions.
A reasonable goal is to choose the distributions so that they keep the same form a posteriori.
Before inference we have a prior distribution p(θ).
After inference we have some new posterior distribution p(θ|x).
We want p(θ|x) to have the same form as p(θ), just with different parameters.

A family of distributions p(θ|α) is called a family of conjugate priors for a family of likelihoods p(x|θ) if, after multiplying by the likelihood, the posterior p(θ|x, α) stays in the same family: p(θ|x, α) = p(θ|α').
The parameters α are called hyperparameters, which are the parameters of the distribution of the parameters.
A trivial example is that the family of all distributions is conjugate to anything, but that is not very interesting.
The form of a good prior depends on the form of the data distribution itself, p(x|θ).
Conjugate priors have been computed for many distributions.
We will give a few examples of conjugate priors.
The conjugate prior for tossing an unfair coin (Bernoulli trials) is the Beta distribution.
The density of the coin’s bias θ is p(θ|α, β) = θ^(α−1) (1−θ)^(β−1) / B(α, β).
If we sample the coin and obtain s heads and f tails, we get p(s, f|θ) = (s+f choose s) θ^s (1−θ)^f.
Then p(θ|s, f) = θ^(s+α−1) (1−θ)^(f+β−1) / B(s+α, f+β).
The conjugate prior for the bias θ of an unfair coin is p(θ|α, β) ∝ θ^(α−1) (1−θ)^(β−1).
After receiving new data with s heads and f tails, the hyperparameters change to p(θ|s+α, f+β) ∝ θ^(s+α−1) (1−θ)^(f+β−1).
This provides a simple learning rule where learning means updating the hyperparameters.
A multinomial distribution with n trials and k categories, where x_i of the experiments fell into category i, has parameters θ_i as the probability of falling into category i.
For the multinomial distribution, p(x|θ) = (n choose x1, …, x_k) θ1^x1 θ2^x2 … θ_k^x_k.
The conjugate prior for the multinomial distribution is the Dirichlet distribution: p(θ|α) ∝ θ1^(α1−1) θ2^(α2−1) … θ_k^(α_k−1).
Upon receiving data x1, …, x_k, the hyperparameters change to p(θ|x, α) ∝ θ1^(x1+α1−1) θ2^(x2+α2−1) … θ_k^(x_k+α_k−1).

For large n+m, θ_ML converges to the true θ.
Suppose only one toss is performed and the result is tails.
Then the likelihood is p(D|θ) = 1-θ.
This likelihood has no interior maximum.
Without a constraint, θ_ML would be -∞.
With the constraint θ ∈ [0,1], θ_ML = 0.
This ML estimate implies the coin will always land tails.
This conclusion is absurd after a single trial.
The mathematics is correct; the missing element is a prior belief about the coin.
A prior is a distribution over θ reflecting beliefs before data.
A uniform prior p(θ)=1 on [0,1] can be used when there is no strong opinion.
With the uniform prior, the posterior (up to normalization) is p(θ|D) ∝ (1-θ).
After normalization, the posterior is p(θ|D) = 2(1-θ) for θ ∈ [0,1].
The MAP estimate with the uniform prior is still 0.
The flat prior does not shift the maximum.
A crucial difference appears when moving from parameter estimates to predictions.
The ultimate goal of learning is not the parameters θ themselves, but making predictions about future data.
For a new coin toss, we want p(heads | D).
The probability p(heads | D) is computed by averaging the likelihood over the posterior.
The formula is: p(heads | D) = ∫_0^1 p(heads | θ) p(θ | D) dθ = ∫_0^1 θ p(θ | D) dθ.
With the uniform prior and D consisting of a single tail, the integral ∫_0^1 θ p(θ | D) dθ gives 1/3, not 0.
More generally, after n heads and m tails under a uniform prior, one obtains p(heads | D) = (n+1)/(n+m+2).
This formula is known as Laplace’s rule of succession.
Laplace’s rule of succession is less extreme than the ML estimate when data is scarce.
Both Laplace’s rule of succession and the ML estimate converge as the number of observations grows.
Full Bayesian inference – keeping the entire posterior distribution and averaging over it – yields smoothed, more cautious predictions that automatically account for uncertainty in the parameters.
For a real coin, our intuition is not a uniform prior.
We expect a real coin to be approximately fair (a bell-shaped curve around 0.5).
If we used a truncated normal distribution as a prior, the posterior would be a product of an exponential and a polynomial – messy to work with analytically.
The key idea is to choose a prior whose functional form looks like the likelihood.
Choosing such a prior makes multiplication easy.
Choosing such a prior ensures the posterior stays in the same family.
Priors with these properties are called conjugate priors.
For Bernoulli trials (coin tosses), the conjugate family is the Beta distribution.
The Beta distribution is: p(θ | α, β) = θ^(α-1) (1-θ)^(β-1) / B(α,β), for θ ∈ [0,1].
α and β are hyperparameters that encode our prior belief.
α = 1, β = 1 gives the uniform distribution.
Larger equal values (e.g. α = β = 10) produce a peak at θ = 0.5, reflecting strong belief in fairness.
If we then observe n heads and m tails, the posterior is also a Beta distribution.
The posterior is: p(θ | D) = Beta(θ | α + n, β + m).
The update rule is simply adding the counts to the hyperparameters.
Bayesian updating with conjugate prior: start with prior Beta(α, β).
After seeing data, the posterior becomes Beta(α + n, β + m).
To incorporate further data D', just use this posterior as the new prior and add the new counts.
The conjugate prior framework naturally connects to regularisation in loss functions.
Taking logs, log p(θ | D) = log p(D | θ) + log p(θ) + constant.
The log-prior acts as a regulariser on the parameters.
If we have k categories instead of two (a multinomial distribution with parameters θ_1, ..., θ_k), the conjugate prior is the Dirichlet distribution.
The Dirichlet distribution is: p(θ | α) ∝ θ_1^(α_1-1) θ_2^(α_2-1) ... θ_k^(α_k-1).
The update for the Dirichlet is: p(θ | x, α) = Dirichlet(θ | α_1 + x_1, ..., α_k + x_k).
Machine learning is, at its core, probabilistic inference: we update our beliefs about model parameters θ given data D using Bayes’ theorem.
The main objects are the likelihood p(D|θ) (the model), the prior p(θ) (our initial belief), and the posterior p(θ|D) (the updated belief).
The two standard point estimates are maximum likelihood (θ_ML) and maximum a posteriori (θ_MAP).
In practice we rarely have infinite data, so the prior matters.
The rational way to make predictions is to average over the posterior, yielding the predictive distribution p(x|D) = ∫ p(x|θ) p(θ|D) dθ.

Choosing a prior from a conjugate family (like Beta for a coin, Dirichlet for multinomial) makes computation trivial: the posterior has the same form as the prior, with hyperparameters updated by simple addition.
These ideas (probabilistic inference, priors, posteriors, conjugate families) are the foundation of all machine learning.
Even when training neural networks with gradient descent, the loss functions we minimise are essentially negative log-posteriors.
Regularisation terms in these loss functions are implicit priors.
